l: the invitation note, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I. A SCANDAL IN BOHEMIA
s: The invitation note tells Holmes that a gentleman will visit him at a specified time to discuss a matter of the deepest importance. It warns that the visitor may wear a mask and is written on distinctive paper later linked by Holmes to Bohemia.

l: the photograph scandal, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I. A SCANDAL IN BOHEMIA
s: The photograph scandal concerns Irene Adler’s possession of evidence of her past relationship with the King of Bohemia. If she sends the photograph when the King’s betrothal is publicly proclaimed, it may end his planned marriage and compromise a reigning European family.

l: the King's planned marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, I. A SCANDAL IN BOHEMIA
s: The King plans to marry Clotilde Lothman von Saxe-Meningen, the second daughter of the King of Scandinavia. He fears that the photograph scandal will cause her family to end the marriage because of its strict principles and her reputation for delicacy.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates Irene Adler by disguising himself as an unemployed groom and gathering information about her home and associates. He learns that Adler frequently sees the lawyer Godfrey Norton and follows them to the Church of St. Monica, where he unexpectedly serves as witness to their marriage. Holmes then recruits Dr. John Watson to assist with a planned operation at Briony Lodge, involving a staged disturbance, a smoke-rocket, and a cry of fire. He disguises himself as a Nonconformist clergyman before setting out for the operation.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Sherlock Holmes spends the morning investigating Irene Adler and Briony Lodge while disguised as an unemployed groom. He gathers information from local horsemen, follows Adler and Godfrey Norton to the Church of St. Monica, unexpectedly witnesses their marriage, and later plans an operation at Briony Lodge with Dr. John Watson's assistance.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Dr. John Watson waits at Baker Street for Sherlock Holmes and listens to Holmes's account of the morning's events. He agrees to assist in the planned operation, remaining near the sitting-room window, throwing in the smoke-rocket at Holmes's signal, and shouting that there is a fire.

l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Irene Adler lives at Briony Lodge, sings at concerts, drives out daily, and is regarded by local men as exceptionally attractive. She travels to the Church of St. Monica and marries Godfrey Norton, then plans to return to her house after driving in the park.

l: Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Godfrey Norton is a dark, handsome, dashing lawyer of the Inner Temple who visits Irene Adler once or twice a day. He hurries to the Church of St. Monica, where he marries Adler with Sherlock Holmes serving as the required witness.

l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Briony Lodge is Irene Adler's two-story villa, built close to the road with a garden behind it. Holmes examines its Chubb-locked door, sitting-room windows, passage window, and coach-house, and later selects it as the scene of his planned operation.

l: Church of St. Monica, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The Church of St. Monica is where Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton go to be married. A clergyman requires a witness because of an informality in their license, and Sherlock Holmes unexpectedly fills that role.

l: the investigation into Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The investigation concerns Irene Adler and the location or protection of a photograph. Holmes examines Briony Lodge, investigates Adler's routine and relationships, and focuses particularly on Godfrey Norton as a possible factor in determining where the photograph may be kept.

l: the compromising photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The photograph is the object Holmes is trying to locate or recover in the investigation into Irene Adler. Holmes considers whether Adler may have transferred it to Godfrey Norton's keeping, but this unit does not establish where it is.

l: the marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton takes place unexpectedly at the Church of St. Monica. Sherlock Holmes is drawn into serving as their witness, and Adler gives him a sovereign afterward.

l: Holmes's disguise as a groom, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Holmes uses the disguise of a drunken-looking, ill-kempt groom to investigate Briony Lodge and learn about Irene Adler from local horsemen and cabmen. In this role, he examines the house and discovers details about Adler's routine and her association with Godfrey Norton.

l: Holmes's disguise as a Nonconformist clergyman, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Holmes changes into the disguise of an amiable and simple-minded Nonconformist clergyman before leaving for the planned operation. His costume, expression, manner, and apparent character are all altered.

l: the planned break-in at Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: Holmes plans an operation at Briony Lodge for the time Irene Adler returns from her drive. He tells Watson that a disturbance will result in Holmes being taken into the house, after which Watson must watch the sitting-room window and act on Holmes's signal.

l: the fire diversion, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The fire diversion is designed to draw attention and create confusion during Holmes's operation at Briony Lodge. At Holmes's signal, Watson is to throw an object into the sitting room and shout that there is a fire, prompting others to repeat the cry before Watson leaves the street.

l: the ordinary plumber’s smoke-rocket, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II.
s: The ordinary plumber's smoke-rocket is a cigar-shaped device with self-lighting caps at both ends. Holmes gives it to Watson to throw into the sitting room when Holmes raises his hand during the planned operation.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Sherlock Holmes and the doctor wait in Serpentine Avenue for Irene Adler to return to Briony Lodge so they can locate a compromising photograph. Holmes and his accomplices stage a street quarrel, fake an injury, and use a false fire alarm to make Adler reveal where she has hidden the photograph. Holmes discovers it is behind a sliding panel above the right bell-pull in the sitting-room, but he postpones taking it until the next morning. As Holmes and the doctor reach Baker Street, an unidentified slim youth addresses Holmes, suggesting that someone may have recognized him.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Sherlock Holmes directs the doctor to carry out a staged street disturbance and a false fire alarm designed to make Irene Adler reveal the photograph's hiding place. He pretends to be injured, is carried into Briony Lodge's sitting-room, and sees Adler reach behind a sliding panel above the right bell-pull. He plans to return with the King at eight the next morning, but postpones taking the photograph because the coachman is watching him.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The doctor waits with Sherlock Holmes in Serpentine Avenue and follows Holmes's instructions during the staged quarrel and false fire alarm. He throws the smoke-rocket into Briony Lodge and later learns how Holmes discovered the photograph's location. He feels ashamed of conspiring against Irene Adler but continues because he believes withdrawing would betray Holmes.

l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Irene Adler arrives at Briony Lodge in her carriage and is caught amid a staged fight outside her house. She permits the apparently injured Holmes to be carried into her sitting-room and responds to the fire alarm by rushing to the photograph's hiding place. She briefly draws the photograph from behind a sliding panel, replaces it after Holmes announces the alarm is false, and then leaves the room.

l: the King of Bohemia, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The King is seeking to recover the photograph and has previously had Irene Adler waylaid and searched. Sherlock Holmes plans to return with him to Briony Lodge the next morning so that he may potentially regain the photograph with his own hands.

l: Serpentine Avenue, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Serpentine Avenue is where the doctor and Sherlock Holmes wait outside Briony Lodge for Irene Adler. Although it is in a quiet neighbourhood, the street is unusually animated with several people who are revealed to be accomplices in Holmes's operation.

l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Briony Lodge is Irene Adler's house and the location where the photograph is hidden. Holmes is carried into its sitting-room after pretending to be injured, and the doctor observes the events through an uncurtained window. Holmes intends to return there with the King the following morning.

l: the compromising photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The photograph is a cabinet-sized object that Irene Adler is unlikely to carry and that both Adler and the client wish to keep from another person's eyes. It is hidden in a recess behind a sliding panel just above the right bell-pull in the sitting-room at Briony Lodge. Holmes locates it but does not take it during the ruse.

l: marriage, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: Irene Adler's marriage to Mr. Godfrey Norton simplifies the situation because she may be as reluctant to let him see the photograph as the original client is to let the King's princess see it. Sherlock Holmes also believes the marriage may soon change Adler's life and habits.

l: staged street quarrel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The staged street quarrel is carried out by accomplices posing as loafers, guardsmen, and other bystanders near Briony Lodge. The fight gives Sherlock Holmes an opportunity to pretend to be struck and injured while the doctor and the other participants make the disturbance appear genuine.

l: the fire diversion, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The doctor throws a smoke-rocket into the sitting-room while shouting "Fire!" after Holmes signals him. The smoke and shouting prompt Irene Adler to rush to the photograph's hiding place, allowing Holmes to see where it is concealed before he declares the alarm false.

l: the quest for the photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter past six when we left Baker Street, and it still
s: The quest for the photograph is practically finished when Sherlock Holmes identifies its hiding place in Briony Lodge. He plans to return with the King and the doctor at eight the next morning, when Adler is expected to be asleep and the house may offer a clear opportunity to recover it.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Sherlock Holmes and the King of Bohemia return to Briony Lodge, where they learn that Irene Adler has married an English lawyer named Norton and left England with him. Holmes finds a photograph of Irene and a letter explaining that she recognized his deception, discovered the King’s intended plan, and fled with her husband. Irene leaves the photograph for the King but promises not to interfere with his plans, while Holmes asks to keep her photograph. The King considers the matter successfully resolved, and Watson concludes that Irene’s wit defeated Holmes’s investigation and prevented a scandal from affecting Bohemia.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Sherlock Holmes returns to Briony Lodge with the King of Bohemia and learns that Irene Adler has left England. He finds her photograph and letter, realizes that she has outmaneuvered him, and asks the King to give him the photograph as his reward.

l: the King of Bohemia, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: The King of Bohemia accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Briony Lodge in search of the photograph. He is relieved when Irene Adler leaves the photograph behind, declares himself immensely indebted to Holmes, and gives Holmes permission to keep it.

l: Irene Adler, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Irene Norton, née Adler, explains in a letter that she recognized Sherlock Holmes’s disguise and discovered the purpose of his investigation. She flees with her husband, keeps the incriminating photograph as protection, and leaves another photograph for the King.

l: Briony Lodge, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Briony Lodge is found with its door open after Irene Adler’s departure. Its furniture, shelves, and drawers are scattered as though Irene searched the house before fleeing, and Holmes finds her photograph and letter hidden behind a sliding shutter.

l: Irene Adler's photograph, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Irene Adler’s photograph is found by Sherlock Holmes at Briony Lodge. Irene leaves it for the King, and Holmes asks to receive it instead; the King agrees.

l: the marriage of Irene Adler and Godfrey Norton, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Sherlock Holmes tells the King of Bohemia that Irene Adler married an English lawyer named Norton the previous day. Irene’s letter identifies her as Irene Norton, née Adler, and says that she loves and is loved by her husband.

l: Irene Adler and Norton's flight to the Continent, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Irene Adler and Norton leave England on the 5:15 train from Charing Cross for the Continent. In her letter, Irene says that they chose flight because they were being pursued by so formidable an antagonist as Sherlock Holmes.

l: the King of Bohemia case, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: The threatened scandal involving the kingdom of Bohemia is prevented when Irene Adler leaves the photograph behind and promises not to interfere with the King’s plans. The King believes that her word is inviolate and that the photograph is as safe as if it were destroyed.

l: Sherlock Holmes's investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Sherlock Holmes’s investigation is intended to recover the photograph that could trouble the King of Bohemia. Although Holmes gains access to Briony Lodge by disguising himself and staging an alarm of fire, Irene recognizes the deception, searches for information about him, and escapes before he can obtain the photograph.

l: Irene Adler's wit, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III.
s: Irene Adler’s wit enables her to recognize Sherlock Holmes’s disguise, determine that he is investigating her, and arrange her escape with Norton. Her cleverness defeats Holmes’s plans, leading Watson to refer to her as the woman.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Sherlock Holmes asks Jabez Wilson to recount how he obtained and lost an unusual position with the Red-Headed League, while Dr. John Watson observes and records the case. Wilson explains that his assistant, Vincent Spaulding, directed him to an advertisement offering a well-paid vacancy to qualified red-headed men. Duncan Ross selected Wilson, who spent eight weeks copying the Encyclopædia Britannica at Pope's Court for £4 a week. The employment abruptly ended when Wilson found a notice stating that the Red-Headed League had been dissolved.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Sherlock Holmes questions Jabez Wilson about the Red-Headed League and asks him to repeat his story in detail for Dr. John Watson. He identifies facts about Wilson's background from his appearance, including manual labor, snuff-taking, Freemasonry, time in China, and recent writing.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Dr. John Watson visits Sherlock Holmes and listens to Jabez Wilson's account. He examines Wilson's appearance, records the newspaper and date, and reads the Red-Headed League advertisement.

l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Jabez Wilson is a red-headed pawnbroker who is recruited into the Red-Headed League after applying for its advertised vacancy. He copies the Encyclopædia Britannica at Pope's Court for eight weeks, earning £4 per week, until he finds a notice announcing that the League has been dissolved.

l: Vincent Spaulding, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Vincent Spaulding works as Jabez Wilson's assistant for half wages and brings the Red-Headed League advertisement to Wilson's attention. He encourages Wilson to apply, helps him get through the crowd at Pope's Court, and says he can look after the pawnbroker's business while Wilson performs the League's duties.

l: Duncan Ross, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Duncan Ross interviews Jabez Wilson, verifies that his hair is genuine, and awards him the Red-Headed League vacancy. He tells Wilson to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica from ten o'clock until two and initially supervises his work before appearing less frequently.

l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Red-Headed League is presented as a fund established from the bequest of Ezekiah Hopkins to provide well-paid, nominal positions for eligible red-headed men. It employs Jabez Wilson for eight weeks before being abruptly dissolved.

l: red-headed men, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Red-headed men over twenty-one who are sound in body and mind are described as eligible for the Red-Headed League. Many red-headed men gather in Fleet Street and Pope's Court to compete for the advertised vacancy.

l: Jabez Wilson's pawnbroker's business, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Jabez Wilson's pawnbroker's business is a small concern at Coburg Square that has declined to the point where Wilson keeps only one assistant. Wilson leaves it during the mornings while he works for the Red-Headed League, relying on Vincent Spaulding to look after it.

l: the Red-Headed League advertisement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Red-Headed League advertisement announces a vacancy paying £4 a week for purely nominal services. It requires eligible red-headed men to apply in person to Duncan Ross at 7 Pope's Court, Fleet Street.

l: the Red-Headed League vacancy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Red-Headed League vacancy attracts numerous red-headed applicants, but Duncan Ross selects Jabez Wilson because his hair meets the required vivid color and he satisfies the other stated conditions. The position requires attendance in the League's office or building from ten to two without leaving.

l: the Red-Headed League employment, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Red-Headed League employment requires Jabez Wilson to copy the Encyclopædia Britannica using his own ink, pens, and paper. He attends daily for eight weeks and receives four golden sovereigns each Saturday.

l: the Red-Headed League dissolution, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Red-Headed League dissolution ends Jabez Wilson's employment suddenly after eight weeks. Wilson learns of it when he finds the office locked on October 9, 1890.

l: the Encyclopædia Britannica, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The Encyclopædia Britannica is the text Jabez Wilson is instructed to copy as part of his Red-Headed League employment. During eight weeks, he copies material from the letter A, including entries such as Abbots, Archery, Armour, Architecture, and Attica.

l: Pope's Court, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: Pope's Court in Fleet Street is the address where red-headed applicants gather and where the Red-Headed League maintains its office. Jabez Wilson works there from ten o'clock until two each day.

l: the dissolution notice, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, II. THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE
s: The dissolution notice is a piece of cardboard fastened to the locked office door. It states, "THE RED-HEADED LEAGUE IS DISSOLVED. October 9, 1890."

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Mr. Jabez Wilson tells Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson that the Red-headed League vanished after costing him a four-pound-a-week position, and Holmes begins investigating. Holmes suspects that Wilson’s assistant, Vincent Spaulding, is central to the mystery after learning about his appearance and examining his trouser knees. Holmes inspects Saxe-Coburg Square and the surrounding businesses, then attends a concert at St. James’s Hall while reasoning about the case. He concludes that a considerable crime is being contemplated and asks Watson to join him at ten o’clock with his revolver.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Sherlock Holmes questions Mr. Jabez Wilson about the Red-headed League, its advertisement, and Vincent Spaulding. He inspects Saxe-Coburg Square, examines Spaulding’s trouser knees, and identifies Spaulding as a highly capable and daring man. Holmes believes a considerable crime is in contemplation and asks Dr. John Watson to help stop it that night.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes while Holmes investigates Mr. Jabez Wilson’s story. He admits that he cannot understand the mystery, attends the concert at St. James’s Hall with Holmes, and agrees to meet him at ten o’clock with his army revolver.

l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Mr. Jabez Wilson explains that the Red-headed League disappeared after he lost a position paying four pounds a week. He says that inquiries led him to discover that the supposed Duncan Ross was actually associated with a man named William Morris, whose stated new address was false. Wilson asks Sherlock Holmes to identify the League and determine why it played the prank on him.

l: Vincent Spaulding, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Vincent Spaulding is Mr. Jabez Wilson’s assistant, hired about a month earlier at half wages because he was handy and cheap. He is described as small, stout-built, quick, clean-shaven, over thirty, marked by a white splash of acid on his forehead, and having pierced ears. Sherlock Holmes recognizes him as a remarkably smart and daring man and examines his trouser knees.

l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: The Red-headed League is the organization that gave Mr. Jabez Wilson work copying the Encyclopaedia and then vanished without explanation. Its supposed officials and addresses proved false, and Wilson lost a position that had paid him four pounds a week.

l: Saxe-Coburg Square, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Saxe-Coburg Square is the shabby location of Mr. Jabez Wilson’s pawnbroking business. Sherlock Holmes studies the square and its surrounding buildings, including the nearby bank, restaurant, shops, and carriage-building depot, because he believes a serious crime may be connected with it.

l: St. James’s Hall, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: St. James’s Hall is where Sarasate performs an afternoon concert. Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson attend the concert, and Holmes spends the afternoon absorbed in the music while continuing to think about the investigation.

l: the Red-Headed League advertisement, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: The advertisement first drew Vincent Spaulding’s attention and led Mr. Jabez Wilson to the Red-headed League opportunity. After the League disappeared, a card or announcement was left on Wilson’s door stating that it had been dissolved.

l: the Red-headed League scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: The Red-headed League scheme gave Mr. Jabez Wilson a temporary position copying the Encyclopaedia and cost him the opportunity to earn four pounds a week when it ended. Wilson regards it as a possible prank costing its perpetrators two and thirty pounds, while Sherlock Holmes suspects that it concealed a more serious purpose.

l: the contemplated crime, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I surveyed this curt announcement and the rueful
s: Sherlock Holmes says that a considerable crime is being planned in connection with the case. He believes there is still time to stop it, but the fact that it is Saturday complicates matters, so he asks Dr. John Watson to assist him at night and bring his revolver.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Sherlock Holmes, Dr. Watson, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather hide in the City and Suburban Bank’s cellar to stop John Clay and his accomplice from robbing French gold. Clay and his red-haired accomplice emerge through a tunnel from Jabez Wilson’s cellar, but Holmes and Jones capture Clay while officers wait for the accomplice. Holmes later explains how the Red-headed League scheme kept Wilson away from his shop while the tunnel was dug. The attempted bank robbery is defeated, and Holmes receives repayment for his expenses and satisfaction from solving the case.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Sherlock Holmes organizes the ambush in the bank cellar and captures John Clay when he emerges from the tunnel. He explains that the Red-headed League scheme was designed to keep Jabez Wilson away from his shop so Clay’s accomplice could dig toward the bank. He concludes that the tunnel was complete and predicts the robbery attempt for Saturday night.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather to the bank cellar and hides there during the ambush. He keeps his revolver ready and witnesses the capture of John Clay. Holmes later explains the case to him at Baker Street.

l: Peter Jones, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Peter Jones joins Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson in the expedition and brings an inspector and two officers to guard the bank’s front door. During the arrest, he grabs at John Clay’s accomplice and later places handcuffs on Clay.

l: Mr. Merryweather, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Mr. Merryweather, a bank director and chairman of the bank directors, leads the group into the bank cellar. He explains that the cellar contains 30,000 napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and helps Holmes guard the bullion.

l: John Clay, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: John Clay emerges from the tunnel with his accomplice and is seized by Sherlock Holmes. He remains cool and sarcastic while being arrested, insists that he has royal blood, and is taken to the police station by Peter Jones.

l: John Clay’s accomplice, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: John Clay’s accomplice, a small, lithe man with a pale face and very red hair, follows Clay through the tunnel carrying or seeking the chisel and bags. He dives back into the hole when Holmes appears, but officers are waiting at the front door.

l: Jabez Wilson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Jabez Wilson is described as a not-over-bright pawnbroker whose presence at his shop is removed for several hours each day. The Red-headed League scheme lures him away so that John Clay’s accomplice can work in the cellar.

l: the Red-headed League, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The Red-headed League is presented as a false organization created to occupy Jabez Wilson while the bank robbery was prepared. Its offices close after the tunnel is completed, signaling to Holmes that the criminals are ready to act.

l: the City and Suburban Bank, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The City and Suburban Bank is the bank whose cellar adjoins Jabez Wilson’s premises. Its unusually large reserve of French gold becomes the target of John Clay’s planned robbery.

l: Baker Street, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: Baker Street is where Dr. Watson meets Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather before the expedition. Holmes and Watson return there after the arrest, where Holmes explains how he solved the case.

l: the bank cellar, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The bank cellar is a heavily secured vault containing crates and massive boxes, including the French gold. Holmes, Dr. Watson, Peter Jones, and Mr. Merryweather hide there and capture John Clay when he breaks through the floor.

l: the tunnel, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The tunnel is dug from Jabez Wilson’s cellar toward the adjoining City and Suburban Bank. Holmes infers its existence from the accomplice’s work in the cellar and uses the evidence to anticipate the attempted robbery.

l: French gold, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The French gold consists of 30,000 napoleons borrowed from the Bank of France and stored in the City and Suburban Bank’s cellar. Its presence motivates John Clay and his accomplice to dig the tunnel and attempt the robbery.

l: bank robbery, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The bank robbery is an attempt by John Clay and his accomplice to reach the City and Suburban Bank’s French gold through a tunnel. Sherlock Holmes, Peter Jones, Dr. Watson, and Mr. Merryweather stop it before the criminals can take the bullion.

l: the Red-headed League scheme, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The Red-headed League scheme uses an advertisement, a temporary office, and a £4-a-week position to draw Jabez Wilson away from his shop. This gives John Clay’s accomplice time to dig the tunnel from the cellar to the bank.

l: the robbery preparations, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, It was a quarter-past nine when I started from home and made my way
s: The robbery preparations include keeping Jabez Wilson away from his cellar, digging a tunnel, and arranging bags and a chisel for the theft. Once the Red-headed League offices close, Holmes realizes the preparations are complete and arranges the ambush.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
s: Sherlock Holmes interviews Mary Sutherland about the disappearance of her fiancé, Mr. Hosmer Angel, who vanished from a cab on their wedding day. Mary explains that Hosmer was a shy cashier who courted her secretly while her stepfather, Mr. Windibank, was away. She believes that an unforeseen catastrophe prevented Hosmer from reaching the church, while Holmes advises her to forget him and agrees to investigate. Mary leaves Holmes four letters from Hosmer, an advertisement, and details about herself and her family.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
s: Sherlock Holmes receives Mary Sutherland as a client and infers details about her short sight and typewriting. He listens to her account of Mr. Hosmer Angel's disappearance, advises her to let the matter become a sealed book, and takes her letters and other papers to investigate.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
s: Dr. Watson is present with Sherlock Holmes during Mary Sutherland's interview. Mary is told that she may speak freely in his presence.

l: Mary Sutherland, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, III. A CASE OF IDENTITY
s: Mary Sutherland consults Sherlock Holmes because Mr. Windibank refuses to involve the police or investigate Mr. Hosmer Angel's disappearance. s: Mary Sutherland and Hosmer Angel become engaged after their first walk together. Hosmer makes Mary swear that she will remain true to him, and they plan to marry quickly while Mr. Windibank is away.

s: James Windibank is Mary Sutherland's stepfather and the man who benefits financially from preventing her marriage. Holmes reveals that Windibank disguised himself as Hosmer Angel, used typewritten correspondence, abandoned Mary at the church door, and then fled Baker Street after being exposed.

s: Mary Sutherland's disappearance of Hosmer Angel is revealed to be the staged abandonment of her supposed bridegroom at the church door. The apparent disappearance was engineered by James Windibank so that Mary would remain emotionally bound to Hosmer Angel and avoid marrying anyone else.

l: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Dr. John Watson joins Sherlock Holmes on a journey to investigate the Boscombe Valley tragedy, in which Charles McCarthy was found dead beside Boscombe Pool. Evidence presented at the inquest strongly implicates Charles’s son, James McCarthy, who was arrested after being found near the body with blood on his hand and sleeve. Holmes considers the circumstantial case serious but believes James’s unusual statements, including references to a rat and a vanishing grey cloth, may support his innocence. Holmes plans to test James’s account personally at the scene.

l: Dr. Watson, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Dr. John Watson receives Sherlock Holmes’s request and travels with him to Boscombe Valley. He reads James McCarthy’s testimony and initially considers the evidence against James extremely damaging.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Sherlock Holmes is asked to investigate the Boscombe Valley tragedy after Inspector Lestrade becomes puzzled. He reviews the reported facts, questions the apparent strength of the case against James McCarthy, and intends to investigate personally while initially assuming that James’s account is true.

l: Inspector Lestrade, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Inspector Lestrade is retained to work on James McCarthy’s behalf but becomes puzzled by the case. He refers the investigation to Sherlock Holmes.

l: John Turner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: John Turner is the largest landed proprietor in the Boscombe Valley area. He made his money in Australia, returned to England, owned Hatherley Farm, and had an only daughter.

l: Charles McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Charles McCarthy was an ex-Australian who rented Hatherley Farm from John Turner. He went to Boscombe Pool on June 3rd for an appointment, was later found dead with repeated blows to his head, and reportedly had a violent quarrel with his son, James.

l: James McCarthy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: James McCarthy, Charles McCarthy’s eighteen-year-old son, was seen following his father toward Boscombe Pool with a gun. He was found near his injured father with blood on his right hand and sleeve, arrested, and charged after the inquest, but he maintained that he was innocent and had left Charles shortly before the fatal attack.

l: William Crowder, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: William Crowder, a game-keeper employed by John Turner, saw Charles McCarthy walking toward Boscombe Pool and James following several minutes later with a gun under his arm. He believed that Charles was in sight of James at the time.

l: Patience Moran, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Patience Moran, the fourteen-year-old daughter of the lodge-keeper, was picking flowers near Boscombe Pool. She saw Charles and James apparently quarrelling, heard Charles use strong language, and saw James raise his hand as if to strike his father.

l: the coroner, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: The coroner questioned James McCarthy at the inquest about the quarrel, the signal “Cooee!”, Charles’s dying words, and the grey object near the body. In concluding remarks, the coroner emphasized discrepancies and omissions that appeared to prejudice James’s case.

l: the coroner's jury, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: The coroner's jury returned a verdict of “wilful murder” after considering the evidence against James McCarthy. James’s remark that his arrest was no more than his deserts helped remove remaining doubt in the jury’s minds.

l: Boscombe Valley, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Boscombe Valley is a country district near Ross in Herefordshire. The tragedy connected with it concerns the death of Charles McCarthy near Boscombe Pool.

l: Hatherley Farm, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Hatherley Farm is a farm held by John Turner and rented by Charles McCarthy. Charles left it on June 3rd to walk toward Boscombe Pool, and James later returned there before being informed that he was under arrest.

l: Boscombe Pool, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Boscombe Pool is a small lake formed by the spreading stream in Boscombe Valley. Charles McCarthy was found dead beside it after being seen there with James during an apparent quarrel.

l: Boscombe Valley tragedy, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: The Boscombe Valley tragedy is the reported killing of Charles McCarthy near Boscombe Pool. James McCarthy was arrested and referred for trial after witnesses and physical circumstances appeared to implicate him.

l: the murder of McCarthy senior, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: Charles McCarthy's murder was apparently committed with repeated blows from a heavy, blunt weapon. The injuries could have been inflicted by the butt-end of James McCarthy’s gun, which was found near the body.

l: the inquest, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: At the inquest, witnesses described Charles and James going toward Boscombe Pool, their quarrel, James’s bloodstained hand and sleeve, and the gun near the body. James testified that he had left Charles alive and returned after hearing a later outcry.

l: James McCarthy's arrest, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: James McCarthy was arrested after returning to Hatherley Farm and being informed by the inspector of constabulary that he was a prisoner. He said he was not surprised and that the arrest was no more than his deserts, but he also protested his innocence.

l: the investigation, The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, IV. THE BOSCOMBE VALLEY MYSTERY
s: The investigation is undertaken by Sherlock Holmes after Inspector Lestrade refers the case to him. Holmes intends to examine the scene and determine whether James McCarthy’s account can be supported.
